entries.clue: Get high on heroin. Injecting one mil makes body spasm (6)

indicatorNotes.on: X on Y means X placed after Y, as a word sits on the one before it in reading order
indicatorNotes.Injecting: to inject is to push something inside, so these letters go into the middle of the others

blocks.note: a millilitre is one cubic centimetre, CC
to get high is to go up

annotation.surface: A grim drugs scene: someone shoots up heroin by the millilitre and their body convulses.
annotation.walkthrough: The full stop after 'heroin' is surface punctuation only. A millilitre is exactly one cubic centimetre, which is how 'mil' becomes two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A hiccup is a plain synonym for a spasm: the diaphragm contracting involuntarily, a jolt of the body.

entries.clue: Image of Billy, his third after wedding vow (4)

indicatorNotes.his third: the third letter of Billy's name

annotation.surface: A photo of a man named Billy, apparently his third marriage portrait.
annotation.walkthrough: 'After' puts Billy's letter behind the vow. 'Third' reads as a third wedding, but it only picks a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: An idol was first a carved image of a god, and still means any image or likeness that is revered.

entries.clue: Linked thing about one English paper's leader (9)

indicatorNotes.about: CHAIN wraps around the other letters

blocks.note: a chain is a thing of links

annotation.surface: Someone describes a linked item carried about by the editor of an English newspaper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Paper's leader' looks like a phrase meaning editor; in fact the 's is 'is', and 'leader' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: The head of a clan is its chief, and a chieftain is simply a leader of a tribe or band.

entries.clue: Beat yak with shortened device (6)

indicatorNotes.shortened: the last letter is cut off

blocks.note: the verb: tap lightly and quickly, as rain does
a device is a design or motif; lose its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone thrashes a yak using a device that has been cut down.
annotation.walkthrough: A triple clue: two definitions and a clipped third, PATTERN losing its N. 'Yak' looks like the animal but is slang for chatter.
annotation.definitionFit: Rain patters, beating lightly on a roof; a salesman's patter is his yak; and a pattern is a decorative device.

entries.clue: Covered decking in preserver and a hardener (8)

indicatorNotes.in: the answer sits inside the following words

blocks.note: the answer runs across the end of 'preserver', through 'and a', into the start of 'hardener'

annotation.surface: Timber decking with a roof, treated with wood preservative and hardener.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a genuine DIY instruction for decking, so the definition sits right at home: VERANDAH runs from preserVER to Hardener.
annotation.definitionFit: A verandah is a roofed platform along the outside of a house, i.e. decking with a cover.

entries.clue: University heads gambling, for example, on probability with second roll-over (4,11)

indicatorNotes.for example: gambling is one example of a vice
indicatorNotes.on: X on Y places X after Y, so CHANCE follows VICE
indicatorNotes.with: 'with' means accompanied by, so the last piece simply joins the end of the others
indicatorNotes.roll-over: rolls S + ROLL over, reversing it

annotation.surface: University bosses betting on the odds, with a lottery rollover coming up.
annotation.walkthrough: A rollover is a lottery jackpot carried forward, which suits the gambling surface; here the hyphen splits it into 'roll' and 'over'. In Britain the vice-chancellor is the working head of a university.
annotation.definitionFit: In British universities the vice-chancellor is the chief executive, the chancellor being ceremonial.

entries.clue: The Listener follows programme on before show again (8)

indicatorNotes.follows: to follow is to come after, so EAR is placed after the rest
indicatorNotes.before: 'before' means in front of, so RE is put ahead of APP

blocks.note: an app is a computer program

annotation.surface: The Listener magazine's crossword appears after some programme, before a repeat showing.
annotation.walkthrough: The Listener is italicised as a publication (also a famous crossword series), but here it is simply the organ that listens.
annotation.definitionFit: To show is to appear, so showing again is reappearing, a plain synonym.

entries.clue: No one wants a student around time of birth (5)

indicatorNotes.wants: needs, so the pieces sit together
indicatorNotes.around: the whole thing goes round T

blocks.note: N for no, as on a Y/N form

annotation.surface: Nobody wants to have a student hanging around them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Time of birth' looks like the definition, but 'time' belongs to the wordplay: the pieces from 'No one' and 'a student' wrap around its letter, leaving 'of birth'.
annotation.definitionFit: Natal is the adjective of birth, from Latin natus, born, as in prenatal and natal day.

entries.clue: Charge copper getting appeal in lawsuit (10)

annotation.surface: A police officer being charged, with an appeal lodged in the lawsuit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is a policeman on the surface, which suits 'charge' and 'lawsuit', but it is the metal.
annotation.definitionFit: An accusation is a charge brought against someone.

entries.clue: Considering everything, one wants to shuffle off this coil (8)

indicatorNotes.shuffle off: the letters of THIS COIL are shuffled

annotation.surface: Hamlet's 'shuffle off this mortal coil': someone taking the long view longs for death.
annotation.walkthrough: The line quotes Hamlet's 'to be or not to be' speech, where shuffling off this mortal coil means dying; here 'shuffle' is taken literally.
annotation.definitionFit: Holistic means treating the whole rather than the parts.

entries.clue: Whip round wearing floppy hat and tie (6)

indicatorNotes.wearing: the whip goes inside the hat
indicatorNotes.floppy: the letters of HAT are rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone passes a hat round for a whip-round, wearing a floppy hat and a tie.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Whip round' reads as a British office collection of money; it splits into a whip (the cat) and a reversal. The blogger saw the Cat in the Hat in it.
annotation.definitionFit: To attach is to tie or fasten one thing to another.

entries.clue: Gloss over what Marie Curie's kids were (6,6)

blocks.note: of a Polish mother and a French father

annotation.surface: Someone skates over the fact of what Marie Curie's children were.
annotation.walkthrough: Marie Curie was Polish-born and married the Frenchman Pierre Curie, so their daughters were French-Polish. 'Gloss over' reads as one phrase; split it.
annotation.definitionFit: French polish is a high-gloss shellac finish for wood.

entries.clue: She was barely noticed riding for £5 in Hackney (4,6)

blocks.note: the legendary naked ride through Coventry, when townsfolk kept their eyes shut
Cockney rhyming slang for a fiver

annotation.surface: A woman rode past almost unseen, for a five-pound fare in east London.
annotation.walkthrough: Legend says Lady Godiva rode naked through Coventry while townsfolk looked away. Hackney is a Cockney area of London, and in rhyming slang a 'Lady Godiva' is a fiver, a £5 note.
annotation.definitionFit: Godiva rode 'barely' clothed, and Lady Godiva rhymes with fiver.

entries.clue: Ditch Harket initially seen fronting Norwegian group (2-2)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the first letter of Harket

blocks.note: a-ha, the Norwegian band of 'Take On Me'

annotation.surface: Morten Harket, singer and frontman of the Norwegian band a-ha, drops everything.
annotation.walkthrough: Harket really does front a-ha, so 'fronting' works on both levels. 'Ditch' looks like a verb meaning abandon; it is the noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A ha-ha is a sunken ditch that bounds a park without blocking the view.

entries.clue: A plant from Panorama ran that clip! (8)

indicatorNotes.from: the answer is taken out of the following words

blocks.note: the answer runs from the end of 'Panorama' through 'ran' into 'that'
surface padding: the exclamation that closes the TV scene

annotation.surface: A TV viewer exclaims that the BBC's Panorama screened a clip of a plant.
annotation.walkthrough: Panorama is the BBC's long-running current-affairs programme; the italics make it a title, but only its letters matter, and AMARANTH starts at its fifth letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Amaranth is a flowering plant, some kinds grown for grain.

entries.clue: Understand fear Nick! (9)

blocks.note: a third definition: anticipate with dread, as in apprehension

annotation.surface: Someone urges a man called Nick to understand what fear is.
annotation.walkthrough: A triple definition. 'Nick' looks like a name; it is the British slang verb for arrest.
annotation.definitionFit: To apprehend is to grasp, to dread, and to arrest.

entries.clue: Labels are ones that don't twist (8)

blocks.note: card players who stand pat in pontoon

annotation.surface: A definition of labels as things that don't twist.
annotation.walkthrough: In pontoon, the British card game like blackjack, a player may 'stick' (stand) or 'twist' (take another card); stickers are those who don't twist.
annotation.definitionFit: Stickers are labels with glue on the back; in pontoon those who stick rather than twist are also stickers.

entries.clue: Happily, after vacation, presidential leader's no longer in charge! Entrancing thought! (8)

annotation.surface: Glee after the holidays that the president is no longer in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vacation' looks like a holiday; in crosswords it means emptying a word.
annotation.definitionFit: Hypnotic means entrancing, as though putting you in a trance.

entries.clue: Ring back and make a disdainful sound (4)

annotation.walkthrough: 'Ring back' reads as returning a phone call; the ring is a hoop.
